_comment: The claims the smoke scenarios prove (#1055). A claim is a short promise with one number, stable forever. Its title is at most
twelve words (#1817); its page under live/smoke/claims/ gives its proofs. Proof is per provider (#1112): each providers.<name> cell
carries a status, an optional note and a list of proofs. A proof is a scenario that runs on that provider (scenario, command, minutes,
needs_go, needs_emulator, real_service, break_mode, evidence, an optional note), some steps of another claim's scenario on the same
provider (proven_by, that scenario's command, a note naming the steps), or a gauntlet stage (stage "<estate>:<stage id>", resolved
against live/gauntlet.json, and a note saying what it asserts). A scenario's header states its cell: "# CLAIM N (provider) - <title>. ~M min.".
demos lists the scenarios that prove no claim; they carry no CLAIM header and belong to no cell.
status is proven (every proof names a dated run: an evidence file with a date, a last_run, steps of such a scenario, or a gauntlet stage that reads pass) or n/a (the substrate has no such concept).
A promise with no proof is a GitHub issue, never a claim.

last_run on a scenario proof is the last result measured for it, carried until a newer run replaces it: status, claim, commit, date (YYYY-MM-DD) and version. live/claims_last_run_test.go holds each entry to this file's history at 958bcf7f2d.
substrate lists the providers the promise applies to: every cell that is not n/a.
retired lists numbers that are no longer claims of their own; a number is never reused. One with claim and provider lives in that claim's cell;
demo: true is a scenario that is now a demo; covered_by names the proof that shows the same thing; merged_into is a whole claim nested in the named one;
reserved: true is a number held back with no claim behind it.
real_service: true marks a proof that runs against the provider's real account, maintainer-run (SMOKE_REAL_AWS=1 for aws).
needs_emulator: true marks a Kubernetes proof that also brings up the pinned floci emulator for an S3-backed record store.
Scenario file names may carry a k8s- prefix for readability. The provider a scenario proves is the providers.<name> key that names its cell, never its file name (#1598, #1593).

claims.title: Owned resources never fall out of a plan

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 manufactures the corruption the claim guards against and passes only by catching it
BREAK=1 manufactures the corruption the claim guards against and passes only by catching it

BREAK=1 sets recovery_window_in_days = 0, which the provider sends as ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery, and requires the opposite outcome - DescribeSecret answering ResourceNotFoundException after the destroy and the replan empty - because without that control the main arm's secret still being there after the destroy would read the same if choudoufu never sent the delete
proofs.note: A scheduled delete (Secrets Manager's DeleteSecret with a recovery window, like KMS's ScheduleKeyDeletion) answers success and leaves the resource in the account, tags included. The plan after it is empty, as stock's is, with no second destroy and no refusal of the swept, still-marked object (#1599).

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 strips the label from the orphan and requires the replan to leave it alone; the ordinary run strips the orphan's address annotation first and requires it to be proposed all the same

BREAK=1 removes the finalizer before the destroying apply and requires the opposite outcome - the object gone in one apply and the replan empty - because without that control the scenario would read identically if choudoufu simply never deleted a ConfigMap

BREAK=1 runs the identical namespace delete and then asserts what a sweep that never saw it would plan, "No changes.", over the real plan; that assertion must fail, and the control passes only when the plan instead proposes the three creates, because without it the creates of step 4 would read the same if the plan proposed them whatever the cluster held
proofs.note: A namespace deleted under a converged estate takes its objects with it, and the plan reads them as gone, the same plan stock makes on the same cluster. Step 7, a deleted record-store namespace, is claim 29's (#1765).

kubernetes.note: The sweep is one cluster-wide, label-selected list per kind, and controller-made objects are excluded before anything reaches a delete. An object no natural key declares is bound by the block its address annotation names (#1640), an orphan otherwise; two objects whose annotations claim one block are refused as a collision (#1641).

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 manufactures the corruption the claim guards against and passes only by catching it

BREAK=1 rebuilds choudoufu from this checkout so the record store's PutObject carries no If-Match (go build -overlay, so it needs Go and cannot break a release binary) and passes only when both racing applies are caught reporting success over one record

BREAK=1 rebuilds choudoufu from this checkout so the store checks every ETag against the payload's MD5 (go build -overlay) and passes only when that binary works under SSE-S3 and fails, on that check and nothing else, under all three KMS flavours
proofs.note: Real AWS, maintainer-run with SMOKE_REAL_AWS=1; it creates four buckets and a KMS key and removes them.

Steps 3 and 10 of claim 29's Kubernetes scenario (#1392, #1441). Step 3 kills an apply with SIGKILL and the next run carries on, with nothing lock-shaped in the records namespace. Step 10 parks two writers' first requests and releases them one at a time: twelve rounds, each landing exactly one write and refusing the other with a VersionConflictError naming both resourceVersions. BREAK=1 swaps each write for the stock backend's read-then-update and requires both writes to land; step 3's control plants a Lease and a lock-named Secret and requires its check to fail.

An unchanged estate planned with -refresh=false serves the objects the sweep vouched for from the cache and skips their reads (65 requests against 74 under CHOUDOUFU_READS=full), with an identical answer.

claims.title: A crash is fixed by re-running

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 strips the ownership markers off everything the killed apply created, leaving the same objects in the same account with no ownership on them; the re-run must then be unable to bind and must build a duplicate VPC, which is stock's behaviour, and a strip that left a marker behind fails the control rather than passing it. BREAK_EARLY_RECORD=1 rebuilds choudoufu with the mid-apply record write switched off (go build -overlay, needs Go, refuses a release binary), so no record is written until the walk is over; the killed run must then leave no record for the inline policy, the password or the effect, the next plan must propose generating the password again, and the re-run must leave two inline policies on the group (#1944)
proofs.note: A record-backed or record-carried instance's record is written the moment its apply step returns (#1944): the killed run leaves records for an aws_iam_group_policy whose name the provider assigned, a random_password and a terraform_data with a provisioner, and the re-run keeps one inline policy, the same password and an effect that ran once. Step 7 deletes the cache, the lock file and the whole .terraform directory, and the next plan from a fresh init is empty.

kubernetes.note: An apply SIGKILLed between one ConfigMap's create and the next leaves one labelled object; the next plan binds it by its label, namespace and name, proposes only what was never reached, and the re-run keeps its uid and replans empty.

proofs.note: The gauntlet's day2_crash stage on a kind estate: an apply creating two ConfigMaps is interrupted by a real SIGTERM the instant the first create commits; the next plan proposes exactly the remainder and binds the created object by its tofu-estate label, namespace and name, matching stock's own plan; one recovery apply finishes and the replan is empty. Its BREAK asserts nothing is proposed and must fail.

claims.title: Identity is a tag you can read, move and carve by

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 manufactures the corruption the claim guards against and passes only by catching it

BREAK=1 strips the label with kubectl and requires live-ls to drop the object from the listing and the replan to refuse it by name, proposing the create the block declares rather than relabelling an object this estate can no longer show it owns; BREAK_ANNOTATION=1 strips the address annotation from an object whose name is read at plan time and requires the replan to refuse that block by name, naming the object, rather than bind it or plan a create over it

BREAK=1 writes spec.replicas = 0 under a CRD that bounds it at minimum 1, a rule only the server checks, and requires the replan refused by name with the server's message quoted and no plan produced; strips the tofu-estate label with kubectl and requires the replan to refuse the CronTab by name and the server's dry run to refuse the create it falls back to, leaving the label off until an operator writes it back; strips it again and removes the block, requiring the replan not to list the object; then deletes the custom resource and requires the replan to propose creating it; and it installs a MutatingAdmissionPolicy that rewrites spec.image on every update, then migrates the stock-made CronTab, requiring live-import to refuse the label write by name ("would also change spec.image"), count it as 1 failed, and leave the object's label and spec untouched; and it then migrates the same CronTab cleanly and cuts manifest_metadata_keys out of the estate's record - the record a build without the migrate-time seed writes - requiring the identical label deletion to plan "No changes." with the label still on the object; and it runs step 14's two-ConfigMap migration under a 60-character estate name, a legal label value, requiring the ratification report to print with one line per ConfigMap and 2 of 2 eligible and the run to exit 0, where the 64-character name was refused once
proofs.note: A custom resource is found again by the apiVersion, kind, namespace and name inside its manifest, carries tofu-estate, and is swept by it; a block whose CRD the cluster does not serve is refused by name; every planned create or update is sent with dryRun=All and the server's verdict printed above the plan; and live-import adopts a stock-made custom resource with one label merge patch, refusing one that would change anything beyond the labels map.

A carve is one label write, tofu-estate=<new> on the object, through live-mv -from-estate or kubectl label; with the admission policy installed the caller must hold both estates, and claim 13's Kubernetes scenario (k8s-the-label-is-the-boundary) measures the refusal without the grant and the carve with it (#1081, item 5).

kubernetes.note: The ownership marker is one label, tofu-estate (#1016); the block address rides beside it in the annotation choudoufu.intentius.io/tofu-address (#1639). Any kubectl reads both. The sweep binds an object no natural key declares to the block its annotation names (#1640). A rename rewrites the annotation; a move between estates is the one label write live-mv -from-estate makes, judged by the admission policy (claim 13 on Kubernetes).

proofs.note: Admission runs after the plan and the server decides what is stored: a fail-closed webhook's refusal is reported in the API server's own words with nothing changed, and the approved plan file applies unchanged once it lifts; a mutating policy that rewrites a declared field reads as stock's perpetual drift while the estate keeps its marker; and a policy that strips the marker on the way in is named by the run that made it.

claims.title: An estate reaches only its own records, and what it declares

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 rebuilds choudoufu from this checkout with the namespace delimiter dropped (go build -overlay, so it needs Go and cannot break a release binary) and passes only when the wire shows the run fetching its neighbour's record

Two controls, each stopping after its own. BREAK=1 has two arms: with the prefix mis-scoped and only the relabel Deny removed, it passes only when the role retags the neighbour's record and then reads it; with the prefix mis-scoped and the read Deny removed, only when the record reads back. BREAK_FIRST_WRITE=1 conditions the write on s3:ExistingObjectTag and passes only when a new estate's first write is denied (claim 34's control). Claim 36's control, a store that sends no tags, was this scenario's BREAK_UNTAGGED=1 arm and is now TestS3StoreTagsEveryObjectItWrites in pkg/staterecord (CI); the arm was dropped under #2288
proofs.note: Real AWS, maintainer-run with SMOKE_REAL_AWS=1; it creates a bucket and IAM roles and removes them. Steps 1, 2, 7 and 8 and the BREAK_FIRST_WRITE arm show a new estate's first record write and the estate tag on every object. The evidence files are the runs of 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-19, us-east-2; the 2026-09-19 run also ran the since-dropped BREAK_UNTAGGED arm.

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 rebuilds choudoufu from this checkout so provisionStoreSentinel returns a denied sentinel write instead of carrying it past to its List (go build -overlay, needs Go), which is what every binary before #1416 did, and passes only when the read-only role then cannot plan at all
proofs.note: Real AWS, maintainer-run with SMOKE_REAL_AWS=1; it creates a bucket and two IAM roles and removes them.

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 renders the consumer's role without --reads-outputs-of network and leaves its configuration declaring the read; the plan must then refuse with "This estate may not read another estate's outputs", naming estate network and the flag, and a plan that shows network's value fails the control
proofs.note: On the pinned emulator with its IAM filter on: an undeclared read is refused by the resource scope of the one statement --reads-outputs-of adds. Non-sensitive, wholly known root outputs cross.

Steps 2, 4, 5 and 9 of claim 29's Kubernetes scenario (#1392). Step 2: a Kubernetes-only estate's first apply writes its first record as a Secret, with no AWS credentials, and the replan reads it back. Step 4: a role scoped to one records namespace reads only that namespace's records. Step 5: every record Secret carries tofu-estate, so the estate-boundary admission policy refuses a write by another estate's identity. Step 9: an identity holding get and list on the record Secrets plans, writes nothing, and is refused the apply naming create, update and delete. BREAK=1 widens the plan role to cluster-wide secret reads and removes the admission policy, and requires the other estate's records to be read and the cross-estate write to land.

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 declares the read and withholds the Role granting get on the producer's output Secret, and requires the plan to refuse naming estate network, its namespace and the Role

kubernetes.note: The declaration is the reader's record_store block: reads_outputs_of "<estate>" {} reads that estate's records namespace through a store that can only get. An undeclared read is refused before anything is sent; a declared read plans with the producer's value and says how old it is; after the producer's destroy deletes its recorded output, the consumer is told so by name.

claims.title: The record store refuses what it can't trust

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 rebuilds choudoufu from this checkout with CheckBucketContract reporting no findings (go build -overlay, so it needs Go and cannot break a release binary), runs one arm against a bucket whose versioning is Suspended, and passes only when that arm's own check catches the apply going through; the scenario's own five arms are the corruptions, one per setting plus a lifecycle that expires nothing and one that expires records

BREAK=1 rebuilds choudoufu from this checkout so the waiver warning is emitted on an estate's first run only (go build -overlay, so it needs Go and cannot break a release binary) and passes only when run two is caught proceeding in silence

BREAK=1 rebuilds choudoufu from this checkout so the bulk read is the one that stood before issue #1355 - the fan-out swallows a failed GET and the map it builds leaves that key out (go build -overlay, so it needs Go and cannot break a release binary) - and passes only when the plan is caught proposing to create a resource that exists. BREAK_CROSSCHECK=1 is step 5's own control: it rebuilds choudoufu without the plan-time call to refuseListedButReadAsAbsent (go build -overlay again) and passes only when, with one record listed and answered 404, the plan is caught proposing to create that instance and apply -destroy is caught reporting 1 destroyed of two with exit 0 and the record still in the bucket, which is GitHub issue #1355's output

BREAK=1 takes the three fences away and requires what they refused to go through: the plan role is given cluster-wide secret reads and must then read the other estate's records, the admission policy is removed and the cross-estate write into a record Secret must then land, and the scoped identity whose first contact the cluster contract passed is given cluster-wide secret reads, after which the same first contact must be refused on read_isolation. A fourth control covers step 10: each racing write becomes the stock backend's read-then-update and all twelve rounds must then end with both writes landed and no conflict named. Steps 11 and 12 each rebuild choudoufu with go build -overlay, as the waiver and bulk-read proofs do on the bucket: a binary whose waiver warning is emitted on an estate's first run only must have its second run refused by step 11's check for naming no waiver, and a binary whose paged listing keeps its first page and drops the error on a later one must be caught by step 12's check exiting 0 with a plan that creates all six resources that exist. Steps 1, 2, 3, 8 and 9 each have a control that runs the step's own check function against a world built to fail it and requires the failure by name: the suite skipped and the suite short one case, the record Secrets stripped of their annotation and then their label, a planted Lease and a lock-named Secret, the Role short one verb given that verb so the same apply goes through and leaves records behind, and a write between the two resourceVersion dumps and a dump of a namespace holding no record; the listings behind steps 3, 8 and 9 are also run through a kubeconfig that reaches no server and must fail rather than read as empty
proofs.note: Steps 6 to 8 and 11 to 12 are this claim: the store checks the records namespace, its RBAC scope, encryption at rest and the estate boundary once, on an estate's first contact, before it writes a record, and refuses each broken assertion by name; a Role one verb short is refused at first contact, naming the verb, with nothing left behind; a waiver names what it waives on every run and `choudoufu live-cluster` ignores it; a listing that fails after its first page fails the plan and never reads as a short estate. Steps 2 to 5 and 9 are claim 28's, and steps 3 and 10 claim 2's.
Step 7 of claim 1's Kubernetes scenario (#1765): the record store's namespace deleted under a converged estate is refused by name on the plan and on the apply, and nothing is written.

claims.title: No secret survives unless you let it

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 applies the same estate under secrets = "store" and runs the identical scan over the identical set of files, which must then find the password (it finds it in the record and the cache); a scan that finds nothing there fails the run, because its zero under refuse would prove nothing
proofs.note: Under refuse the argument is proposed on every plan, rotated or not, and the scenario asserts both arms (#1503).

kubernetes.note: Under strict { secrets = "refuse" } on a kind cluster, a random_password is refused by name with nothing written, a kubernetes_secret_v1 fed from the environment applies with no state cache and the value in no kept file, and the replan is empty because the API server returns the data; a rotated value is proposed (#1873).

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 applies the identical estate under secrets = "store" and runs the identical scan, which must find the value (it finds it in the state cache); a scan that finds nothing there fails the run, because its zero under refuse would prove nothing

BREAK=1 removes the estate's own ignore_tags declaration - the one piece of configuration the claim is about, not a choudoufu code path - and runs the identical out-of-band AWS CLI tag write; it passes only when the plan now proposes an update naming the tag, because choudoufu has no tag-diffing of its own to defeat with a build overlay: a resource's tags are planned entirely by the real hashicorp/aws provider process, the same one a stock run talks to
proofs.note: A tag another account's automation or an AWS service adds out of band churns nothing once the estate tells its provider to ignore that key, and an edit to a tag the estate declares plans (#1624).

proofs.break_mode: BREAK=1 runs the identical kubectl command against a key the configuration does NOT declare - same object, same --overwrite, one key different - and requires the opposite outcome, "No changes.", with the label still on the object afterwards. Without it every plan the main arm requires would read the same if choudoufu simply planned on any difference between the configuration and the live object, and step 5's point - that the provider's computed_fields rule still keeps the server's own keys out of the plan - would be scenery. It then runs one control for steps 8 and 9 together: the same two working directories on record_store "local", where the second one has no record to read and must plan "No changes." instead of the removal, which is what a Kubernetes estate on the implied store gives its second operator today.
proofs.note: A key the configuration never declared (the API server's kubernetes.io/metadata.name, a controller's annotation) stays the server's and churns nothing, because kubernetes_manifest's computed_fields reads the prior manifest. A label or annotation edited, added or deleted in the configuration plans the one in-place update stock plans, and a second working directory with no record of its own removes the same label when the estate shares its records.
